scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Recognized in the 1970s in the United States, aerial dance grows from modern dance's desire to explore three-dimensional space.
Trisha Brown's 'equipment pieces' from 1968 to 1971 are foundational, placing dancers on side walls to recontextualize pedestrian movement.
Terry Sendgraff's 1970s 'motivity' trapeze introduces single-point suspension, enabling rotational movement.
on_screen: Map: United States · Global
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Aerial dance is performed at arts festivals, in contemporary circus, and as site-specific installations.
It explores themes of weightlessness, freedom, and the human relationship with architecture.
For practitioners, it represents a 'place where everything is possible,' breaking the constraints of floor-bound movement to communicate contemporary ideas through an altered state of gravity.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:VideoCervantino 1.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b9/VideoCervantino_1.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers utilize suspended apparatuses to perform wraps, inversions, and drops.
In vertical dance, performers in harnesses use walls as floors, executing leaps and runs perpendicular to the ground.
In silk work, dancers climb using French or spiral ascents and secure themselves with keys around the waist or feet.
Watch for Kamikaze and Star drop.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Three-dimensional; utilizes vertical, horizontal, and diagonal paths.

While no specific genre is mandated, contemporary scores, electronic music, and theatrical soundscapes are common.

The soundscape features sweeping electronic or orchestral textures that emphasize the scale of the vertical space, punctuated by rhythmic beats that cue drops or transitions.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Settings range from traditional theaters and circus tents to office buildings, bridges, and canyons.
Costumes are form-fitting to avoid entanglement with ropes or silks; acetato deportivo or jersey fabrics are common for the apparatus itself.
Safety equipment is a critical part of the setting, including crash mats, carabiners with screw locks, and swivels to allow for 360-degree rotation without twisting the lines.
on_screen: Image gallery: 5 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Trisha Brown is a pioneer of equipment pieces, Terry Sendgraff is the inventor of the motivity trapeze, Joanna Haigood is a site-specific researcher, Amelia Rudolph founded Project Bandaloop, Wanda Moretti created the vertical dance network, and Isabelle Chassé is an aerial silk pioneer.
The Boulder style in Colorado is known for its annual festival and workshops.
The form derives from a combination of modern dance, traditional circus arts including Spanish web and static trapeze, and rock climbing.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Aerial dance is a parent of modern dance, serving as a subgenre that applies modern dance aesthetics to vertical space.
Aerial dance is a variant of aerial silk, a specific discipline using fabric.
Aerial dance is a variant of bungee dance, utilizing elastic cords for high-rebound movement.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Keep an engaged core with elongated limbs, requiring hollow body positioning for inversions.
Maintain high grip strength, using arms for pulling during ascents and stabilizing during poses.
